titleStmt.title: Observations on Textual Points Raised by the United Kingdom Government in Memorandum Enclosed in Note of January 21, 1947

div.head: Observations on Textual Points Raised by the United Kingdom Government in Memorandum Enclosed in Note of January 21, 1947
div.p: By its second recital the United States, of course, does not claim to be in the islands as a mandatory power but it recognizes that it is administering islands which formerly were under mandate. These islands were militarily taken from Japanese forces, but since, in our view, they did not belong to Japan, they could not legally be taken away from Japan. Hence, they do not completely fit the category of Article 77(b) (enemy territory). However, no difficulty is seen in clarifying the point that the United States is not in these islands now as a mandatory power.

The United States considers that in a strategic agreement security factors take precedence over economic factors. Moreover, it is not believed that there is any inconsistency with the provisions of the Charter. It is not the intention of the United States to seek any economic advantage for itself but merely to provide the necessary protection for areas which may need to be closed.

The United States considers that the proposed regulation on traffic rights to aircraft flying into and out of the trust territory is precisely in accord with the Chicago Aviation Convention and that the same situation would apply whether Article 8, paragraph 3, were included in the draft or not.
This proposal appears to state the position somewhat more precisely in terms of Article 83(3) of the Charter and will be carefully studied by the United States.

The United States takes the view that the territory to be placed under trusteeship by the draft agreement is the same area as that under mandate to Japan and that the territorial waters included in the trust territory would be determined by customary interpretations of international law.
